This mostly looks fine @Schnorg although I'm slightly concerned about going through the `HashMap` twice as this may not be fast and can likely be avoided. It kind of depends how big and how slow this `HashMap` is likely to get in worst case scenarios.

Maybe on the first pass you can:
* do the first pass operation
* add items that are only needed for the second pass to a secondary `LocalVector` (maybe static, depending on whether this is multithreaded code, as we want to avoid allocations)
* do the second pass via the `LocalVector`.

Other options, if the size of the hashmap isn't that great (i.e. won't blow the stack):
* use `alloca` to allocate a temporary array to store the second list on the stack - this avoids the cost of allocation
* search for `alloca` in the engine to see examples of use if you haven't used it before

> The HashMap looks as fast as I would hope for (for iteration), with all the elements chained in a simple linked list. 

We don't use linked lists where possible in performance sensitive code - for exactly these reasons, and that's why in core we've tried to migrate away from them. They can be one of the slowest containers to use on modern CPUs because each link in the chain is potentially jumping around in cache.

Having said all this, it comes down to how many elements are expected to be in the `HashMap`, and how often it will get hammered. They may for example already be in cache anyway because of the first traversal, this kind of thing often needs profiling.

It's likely this can be investigated as a followup performance PR if you aren't keen.

> One cost that I don't love is the HashMap remove() function. When I call remove() with an Iterator, it feels to me like it should be able to just remove the element immediately, since the Iterator already holds a valid reference to the element to be removed. However it instead grabs the key from the Iterator and does a fresh lookup, and then removes it. This seems costly, but there is probably a good reason it is necessary.

I had a little look at this, and it seems a consequence of the Robin hood hashing implementation in the `Hashmap`, maybe the iterator doesn't have enough information _in itself_ to do the erase efficiently. But I'm not super familiar with the template (I did review it at the time, but it was years ago).

Now whether it is the _best_ container to use for this particular task is another matter...
Godot uses a lot of hashed containers. I've very rarely ever needed to use them myself when writing high performance code over decades... make of that what you will.

Another concern with these HashMaps (and similar ones on the Scene side) was when I noticed they were using the default allocator and allocating for every element. Hence this 'optimisation' PR:

[Replace DefaultAllocator use in area monitoring HashMaps - #122614](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/122614)

I think it is a fair bit of work to try to figure out and potentially refactor to replace these HashMaps, so I would leave that for a potential future performance or clean up PR.

I did have a brief look at this tonight, and added some asserts to check that their fast lookup functionality is needed. I think in the future, if we fix enough other logic and timing issues, then the need to do a lookup before adding an overlap report could go away entirely and then LocalVectors would be better in every way.

I also like keeping them for the moment because they could be useful for future refactoring. My first thoughts for eliminating them tends to require that the upstream code works in a certain way (or the right way), so if we got rid of them (in the way I am thinking), the rest of the code would be harder to refactor as the reporting would be more reliant on how the upstream code works. 

For example I can see a future where the physics step runs multiple times, or sub-steps between callbacks (rather than just once), in which case we would value the buffering.

*TLDR - After working on this more, I still conclude it's best to do a subsequent performance PR as I don't have a satisfying answer in a hurry.*

There is one issue with using a LocalVector for these lists, which is that those containers will never compress, and if they did compress, it would be causing default allocations during physics frames on a regular basis (since neither of them can accept a custom allocator). 

If there was just one LocalVector for all areas to share, then this would be fine. The LocalVector would grow to the size of the maximum number of collision changes per frame.

Let's say there are 1000 areas and 1000 maximum collision changes per frame. If you have a horde move through one area, it will grow that one area's LocalVector to 1000, but then the horde will move on to the next area and grow it's LocalVector to 1000, and so on. 

So since the LocalVector is not shared, instead of an array of the size of 1000 elements and maybe 10 total allocations, you eventually get 1000x these arrays, or memory allocated for 1,000,000 elements with 10,000 default allocations made, even though you only ever need 1000 elements in your lists in any one frame. I am not sure how bad that is,  but I suspect that this would waste physical memory (not just virtual memory) due to fragmentation.

Also, these lists are stored per area and so there is no fast path to a stable size. LocalVector size stability will only be reached when every area in the entire level has been maximally interacted with. Again, if it were a vector shared amongst all areas, we would get to size stability with far less allocations.

*NOTE: If these things are issues for the area monitoring, then they may be issues for the BVH as well, since it is using a LocalVector per object for pairing.*

Alternatively if you use HashMaps, and you have them all share the same static PagedAllocator [as done here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/122614), then the PagedAllocator only grows to what is needed for 1000 elements (not a worst case of 1,000,000). Though you then have pointer chasing (hopefully mostly around L3 cache and not across main memory).

There are HashSets...but like a LocalVector, they do not accept custom allocators to reduce the default allocator problem.

I am tying myself in circles with this at the moment, so probably still best to optimise in a subsequent PR or for someone more experienced with container and hardware nuances to take this to the next level. 

I think the ultimate solution actually still hinges on upstream refactoring. Namely, I think narrow phase needs to link more closely with broad phase, and that could improve the order of what emerges from the 'collision' system.

At the moment, Godot is building constraint islands out of broadphase results, when it should be doing this only after narrow phase results. This (to my mind) is an error, and it is killing solver performance, and narrow phase performance, and downstream logic / wake / sleep outcomes at the same time. To fix it requires a relatively chunky refactor that no one would love to review :(.
Yup it's fine to leave for a follow up, just to note that it is likely not optimal and something we can improve. :+1:
